content: Hello, and thank you for taking the time to talk with me. I’m a researcher who conducts interviews about people’s lives, and there are no right or wrong answers — you’re welcome to skip anything you’d rather not discuss. To begin, I’d love to hear about your life. Could you tell me the story of your life, starting from wherever you’d like?

huh, the whole thing? that's a lot to fit in a text message
ok. i grew up about eight miles outside a town of like 550 people in northeast PA. dirt road, firewood, school bus. my dad drove the bus and sold firewood, mom worked at a bank. that's the short version of the first eighteen years
then i went to college for art, mostly because i was good at drawing and didn't know what else to do with it. graphic design, which sounded more practical than it turned out to be
That's a vivid start — the dirt road, the school bus, the firewood. What was it like growing up out there, in a town that small?

quiet, honestly. everybody knew everybody, which was both a good and a bad thing
like you couldn't get away with much, but if your truck broke down someone would just show up with a chain without even asking. i miss that part
mostly i remember being outside a lot. helping dad with the firewood, that was kind of the family thing. i was the younger one so i got the easy jobs at first, stacking and not the splitting
You mentioned being the younger one — tell me about your family, who else was in the house growing up?

just the four of us. me and my older sibling — we were close as kids and then kind of drifted the way you do, different lives and all that
mom and dad are still in the county actually. dad's basically retired from the bus but still cuts firewood because he can't sit still. mom's out of the bank now
So you left that dirt road for art school. What was that transition like — going from a town of 550 to studying graphic design?

honestly the first school wasn't much of a leap. williamsport's just a bigger town, not exactly the big city. but i didn't really know what i was doing — started at penn college for a year, kind of spun my wheels, took a semester off
then i ended up at mansfield for the actual degree. that felt right, smaller, i knew how to be in a small place
the real jump was later, when i moved to philly. that one actually scared me
Sounds like Philly was the real threshold. How did that move come about, and what was it like landing there?

i wanted to see if i could actually do this design thing somewhere that mattered. towanda sign shops weren't gonna tell me that
i got a couple short contracts at small agencies. short is the word — a few months here, a few months there. and i worked retail evenings to make rent, which is a fun combination
landing there was rough at first honestly. like loud and fast and nobody waiting on you. i remember my apartment had a radiator that clanked all night. took me a while to find my people, and some of that i never did
You said it took a while to find your people — and some of that you never did. What did finding people look like there, and who ended up mattering to you?

slow, honestly. i'm not a natural joiner. bars, some people through work, the whole philly thing of roommates of roommates
there was one person who mattered a lot back then. we were together a long time. that's kind of its own story and not a happy-ending one, so, i don't know. maybe we save it for later if it comes up
Fair enough — we'll leave that where you put it for now. Let me ask about your life these days: what does a normal day look like for you, from waking up to going to bed?

depends on the day, my work's a patchwork so there's no real template. but like a normal weekday — up around 6:30 because the kids are up, get them out the door to school, that's the fixed point
then it's whatever the week is. some days it's freelance stuff on the laptop, some days i'm out painting a sign or installing one, and one day a week in the fall and spring i'm teaching at the community college
partner works at a vet clinic in towanda so her schedule's more real than mine
evenings is dinner, kids, garden in the summer, and honestly a lot of nights i'm out at a fire hall with the band or in the basement with the bass when there's no gig
That's a lot of moving parts — patchwork work, kids, and then the band on top of it. Tell me about the band and the bass; how did music become part of your life?

late, honestly. i was in my thirties before i really picked one up. a buddy needed a bass player and i couldn't play a lick, but i could keep time, so i faked it till it was sort of true
i never had lessons or anything. i'm not gonna pretend i'm some musician. i'm a guy who knows where the root note is and stays out of the way, which is honestly 80% of playing bass in a cover band
we play fire halls and county fairs, which i love. like it's not glamorous but when a fire hall's packed and everybody's drunk and dancing to something we're kind of half-assing... that's a good feeling. it's the closest i get to feeling like i'm from one thing instead of five
"Closest I get to feeling like I'm from one thing instead of five" — that's a striking way to put it. What do you mean by the five?

ha, i don't know, it just kind of came out. but like — designer, sign painter, teacher, band guy, dad. that's five
and none of them is a full-time thing, you know? i'm not the guy at a studio, i'm not a full-time professor, and my band's not my job. so i'm always kind of half in each one
some days that's fine and it keeps things interesting. other days it feels like i'm not really from anywhere. the band's the one place it doesn't feel split, i guess because nobody there cares what else i do

That makes sense — the band being the place where nobody needs you to be anything else. I want to understand how the patchwork came together: is it something you chose, or something that happened to you piece by piece?

piece by piece, mostly. i'd love to say i designed it, but no — i just kept taking the next thing that paid and could fit around the other things
sign work turned into the shopper newspaper layout turned into the camp marketing turned into teaching. none of it was a plan, it was just the next check
there's a freedom in it i actually like. but ask me in january when the quarterly taxes are due and i might give you a different answer
i guess the honest version is i chose the freedom and the freedom came with the rest of it. can't really have one without the other
You mentioned the quarterly taxes — let's talk about money a bit. How does it actually work, making ends meet across all those pieces?

honestly? it's a juggling act and my partner's the steady one. she's got the real job with the clinic, benefits and all. mine's the pile that adds up but never the same twice
i keep a spreadsheet, invoice everything, put money aside for taxes every time a check comes in. i've been doing it long enough that it's just habit now. the bad months are usually winter, sign work dries up when it's cold
the teaching's the closest thing to reliable, one class a semester, but adjunct pay is... not a lot. the shopper paper's steady-ish. everything else comes and goes. you learn to make a fat month cover two thin ones
That habit of making a fat month cover two thin ones — can you walk me through what a thin month actually looks like? What gets cut or deferred?

it's less dramatic than it sounds. nothing gets "cut" exactly, it's more deferring. the truck needs brakes, well, it can wait another month. the furnace, the dentist, new boots for the kid, all of it slides to the right
the garden helps in summer, we eat a lot out of that. winter's the pinch. but honestly we get by, i don't want to make it sound grim. it's more like never quite catching your breath than actually falling

That phrase — never quite catching your breath rather than actually falling — I understand. Speaking of the house and the furnace, tell me about where you live now. How did you end up in that place, in that town?

came back in 2014 after living in england for a stretch, and just sort of... stayed. it wasn't a plan, it was supposed to be temporary
it's a rented farmhouse outside town, old place, drafty in spots. the landlord's decent which is rarer than it should be. but the garden behind the house is what sold me, and it's quiet out there
i've thought about buying a place, but the math on a patchwork income for a mortgage... the bank looks at you like you're joking. so rented it is for now
You mentioned living in England for a while — that caught me. What took you there, and what brought you back?

a studio gig, sort of. it wasn't a big career move, it was more like I knew someone who knew someone and there was a small studio that needed an extra pair of hands
i was there maybe a year and a half? Bristol. did design work for them, pulled bar shifts to make rent, same as I was doing here basically but with a different accent around me
came back in 2014 because the money ran thin and honestly I missed the quiet. the novelty wears off and you're just a guy doing layouts in a city where your whole family's an ocean away
Coming back to the quiet after Bristol — did that feel like coming home, or more like retreating?

both, if i'm honest. it was home in the way it's always home, familiar, the woods, people who know my parents
but yeah, some of it was retreating. the money wasn't working, i was tired, and i came back to the safe thing. i don't think i admitted that to myself for a couple years
and then the year after i got back my long relationship ended, so that stretch wasn't exactly me landing on my feet. it was more like landing on the ground, which is different
You mentioned earlier that relationship was a story you might save for later — and now you’ve touched on it yourself. If you’re willing, tell me what that ending was like for you.

it was seven years. it ended in 2015. no big blowup, nobody cheated, nothing dramatic. it just slowly stopped working and then one day we both knew it was done
which somehow makes it harder in a way. there's nothing to be angry at. it just didn't hold. i was pretty low for a while after. didn't do much of anything for a stretch there
that's about as much as i've got in me on it right now, if i'm being straight with you

That's fair — thank you for going as far as you did with it. Let me turn to the life you've built since: you mentioned your partner works at the vet clinic and you've got kids. How did the two of you come together?

a friend's cookout, kind of, but the real meet was she came out to a show. i was still kind of a mess in 2016, honestly, not in a great place
she looked like she'd rather be anywhere else and then she stayed till the last song, so i figured there was something there. took me way too long to actually ask her out though. she'll tell you i was slow about it
and then it just... fit, in a way the other one never quite did. different pace. quieter. she's steady and i'm the patchwork, so we kind of balance out. i'd be lying if i said that didn't matter
You said she's steady and you're the patchwork, so you balance out. Tell me about the kids — what's family life like day to day with them?

chaos, mostly in a good way. nine and six. one of them's got my stubborn streak and the other's got her mom's calm, so there's a little of each of us running around the house
honestly the tired is real. i'm 41 with a six year old, i'm not the young dad at the school events. but they're funny little people and they say stuff that cracks me up
the six year old's really into bugs right now, like obsessed. there's a jar situation in our kitchen that i have opinions about
The jar situation — I have to ask. What's living in the kitchen these days?

currently i think we're between jars. the last one was a lizard that i'm pretty sure wasn't gonna make it, and i was the one who had to have the talk about that, fun times
the rule now is bugs go back outside same day. she negotiated me down from "no jars" to "same day," which honestly shows she's got a future in something
She negotiated you down — that's a good kid. Let me shift a bit: how are you doing these days, in yourself? Health, energy, sleep, stress — however you'd put it.

that's a question nobody asks me, huh
tired more than i used to be, if i'm honest. sleep's not great, i'm up thinking about the invoices or the truck or whatever at 2am sometimes. the money stuff sits in the back of my head like a hum you stop noticing until it's real loud
but i'm alright. better than i was a few years back, that's for sure. garden keeps me level in the summer, trout fishing in spring, band year round. i've got my things
When that hum gets loud at 2am, what do you do with it — is there anything that actually helps?

not that productively, honestly. i get up and make a list, try to turn the hum into something concrete i can look at. sometimes that helps, sometimes it's just anxiety with better handwriting
the thing that actually works is fixing one small thing. send the invoice, make the call i've been dreading. then it quietens down for a night. i've just never figured out how to put it down without doing something first
and a beer sometimes, which i know isn't the answer. mostly the list though
You mentioned the fire hall and the band, and the small town where everyone shows up with a chain — I'm curious what community means to you now. Where do you feel most like you belong these days?

the band, probably. that's where i'm just mike and nobody wants anything from me. fire halls, county fairs, a bunch of guys older than me playing songs that were old when we learned them
but there's something about being back in the county where my parents are too. like i'm the kid on the dirt road and the 41-year-old with kids at the same time. it's a weird feeling, kind of grounding and kind of claustrophobic depending on the day
the garden's its own thing. that's where i'm just with my hands in the dirt and my head finally shuts up a little
That tension between grounding and claustrophobic is interesting — what makes it feel claustrophobic on the bad days?

it's the everybody-knows thing. i came back at 32, broke, single, living in my parents' county again. and in a town this size, people kind of freeze you at that
like i'm always going to be the guy who went away and came back. nobody says it, but you feel it. and some days you just want to walk into a store and be a stranger for once
the band doesn't feel like that though. weirdly the band's the exception. maybe because it's loud enough to drown all that out

"It's loud enough to drown all that out" — I like that. Let me ask something a bit bigger: what matters most to you now, in terms of how you try to live? That could be values, faith, or just the things you'd want your kids to learn from you.

not a church guy, so i don't have a tidy answer for this one
but the thing i keep coming back to is do it right even when nobody's checking. that's the sign work talking, kind of. the prep behind a sign, nobody ever sees it, but the sign's either gonna hold for ten years or it isn't based on that and nothing else. i think about that a lot
and show up when you said you would. that one's simple and most people don't do it. that's mostly what i'd want the kids to pick up from me, if they pick up anything
That's a good answer, not a tidy one. Let me ask about the future: when you picture the next five years, what do you hope for — and what worries you?

the hope part's not complicated. kids healthy and halfway decent humans, me and her still liking each other, maybe a place of our own finally
the worry's the boring one. i'm 41 and there's no retirement worth the name, nothing like a real job would've given me. and patchwork at 46 is the same patchwork with older knees and the same truck that needs brakes
i try not to stare at it too long. but yeah, that's the thing that hums at night more than anything

That hum about the future — I hear it. Let me go back to something earlier: you studied graphic design partly because it seemed practical. Looking back, how do you feel about that choice now — the art school path?

funny you say practical, because it wasn't really. it was practical compared to fine art, i guess, i told myself that
but look at it now — i paint signs by hand and teach one intro class. the degree got me in the door at sign shops and it taught me to see, which matters. but "practical" was kind of a story i told my parents and myself
i don't regret it. i'd probably have been miserable as an accountant. but there's a version where i learned a trade and had benefits and my knees would thank me. i think about that sometimes, especially in january
Let me ask about the flip side of all that: what are you proudest of, looking back over the last twenty years or so?

honestly? that i built a life back after a bad couple of years, and didn't just... quit on the whole thing. nobody handed me the life i've got now, i pieced it together after coming home broke and single
and the band, weirdly. i picked up an instrument in my thirties with no lessons and now i can play a whole night at a fire hall and people dance. that one's mine entirely
the kids too, but i can't take all the credit there, half of that's her being the steady one
That's a lot to be proud of — building it back, and the bass being entirely yours. If you could sit down with yourself at 22, just starting out, what would you tell him?

he wouldn't listen, honestly. nobody at 22 listens. but i'd tell him to stop treating every job like a stepping stone to some "real" life that's always about to start
the in-between years were the actual life, and i spent a lot of them waiting for the real one to show up
and learn how money works way earlier. i was basically guessing at taxes and invoices till my thirties. also maybe don't be so scared of looking like a beginner. that one cost me some years too

"Don't be so scared of looking like a beginner" — that's one I think a lot of people would want to hear earlier. Let me ask one more thing about the bigger picture: how do you see the country and the wider world these days, and where you and your family fit in it? Only if you're comfortable going there.

honestly i don't think i fit neatly into either version of the country people are always arguing about on tv. i'm rural but i'm not, i don't know, i don't check all the boxes people assume when they hear northeast PA
i mostly think about it small. my town, my kids' school, whether the people around me are doing okay. the big picture stuff, i've kind of stopped trusting anyone who's real sure about it
i'll say this much — it feels more divided than when i was a kid, and the town's changed in ways i can't quite put my finger on. some of it for the better, some of it not. that's as far as i want to wade in, if that's alright

That's more than alright — you've waded in as far as you want, and that's fine. I'm curious about one thing you said, though: the town's changed in ways you can't quite put your finger on. What have you noticed shifting?

little stuff mostly. there were way more small farms when i was a kid, now it's bigger operations and a lot of that ground leased out
more gas trucks on the roads than there used to be, more people commuting out to work instead of working in town. the school's still holding on, that's something. but half the kids graduate and don't come back, which, i mean, i did and i'm kind of the exception
and prices everywhere, wages not so much. that's the one that actually hits people day to day. i'd probably sound like an old man complaining about it, but it's real

That's not just an old man complaining — those are real shifts. I think we've touched nearly everything I hoped to. Before I wrap up: is there anything important about your life that I haven't asked about, something you'd want a stranger to understand about you?

i think i'd want a stranger to understand it's not a sad story. i know it sounds like a lot of hum and thin months and juggling, but it's not a sad story
it's a messy one. i've got a partner i like, two funny kids, a bass and a garden and a fire hall full of people who don't care what else i do. that's a lot more than a lot of people get
and nobody hands you the tidy version anyway. the messy one was the real one the whole time. i think that's what i'd want on the record, if there's a record

I'll put it on the record exactly that way: not a sad story, a messy one — and the messy one was the real one the whole time. That's a fine thing to have said, and I'm grateful you took the time to say it to me. Thank you for talking with me so openly about your life, Mike — the dirt road, the patchwork, the bass, all of it. I wish you and your family well.
